amendments.rule: **A verb the ASV renders as a light verb plus a complement heads on the complement, not on the light verb.** This is rule 31's test applied to a verb: drop each word in turn, and the head is the one whose loss loses the lexeme. `הַאֲזִין` → *Give ear unto* heads on *ear*, because *give* alone gives anything; so too `הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה` → *did obeisance*, `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel*, `הִמְלִיךְ` → *make king*, `הוֹדָה` → *give thanks*, `כִּלָּה` → *made an end*, `עוּד` → *bear witness*, `חָנַן` → *make supplication*, `בּוֹשׁ` → *put to shame*. The complement need not be a noun: an adjective (`הִכְבִּיד` → *made heavy*, `גָּדַל` → *make greater*) and a second verb (`חָטָא` hiphil → *made to sin*, `אָכַל` → *did eat*) are read the same way. Rule 24's *lexical predicate over subjects and auxiliaries* is about `was gathered`, and must not be read as a preference for the English verb — that reasoning would head *make king* on *make*. **A phrasal particle is not a complement.** `שָׁלַח` → *put forth*, `סוּר` → *take away*, and `נָתַן` → *put away* are one lexical verb plus its particle, and the head stays on the verb; the same subtraction says so, since *forth* and *away* alone name nothing. **But run that same subtraction on the particle before folding it in.** Where the bare English verb already writes the source verb's whole lexeme and the particle adds a direction, a result or a repetition the Hebrew does not write, no morpheme licenses that word: it is its own `added` unit under rule 30 and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering, exactly as this rule leaves a supplied object noun `added` and rule 17 a supplied lexical subject noun. `שׁוּב` → *turn ... again* keeps its *again* with the verb, discontinuous under rule 25, because *turn* alone does not write the returning, and `כָּנַס` → *gather ... together* and `מָצָא` → *find out* keep theirs on the same ground; but `בּוֹא` hiphil → *bring him* ***back*** leaves the *back* `added`, because the hiphil is the bringing and *bring* has already written it. An ASV italic on such a particle corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. Read the source verb's lexeme against the bare English verb rather than the shape of the English verb phrase, since the particle of *put forth* and *take away* is what completes a lexeme neither *put* nor *take* writes, and do not fold a surplus particle into the verb, the object or a preposition standing beside it, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*. **A supplied object is not a complement either, and that holds of any verb's rendering and not only a light verb's.** Where the ASV writes an object pronoun inside or beside a Hebrew verb's rendering — `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let* ***it*** *fall*, `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave* ***them*** *drink*, `אֲנִי שָׁמָעְתִּי` → *I have heard* ***it*** — read whether an object morpheme is present. Where one is, it takes the pronoun under rule 18 and the verb keeps the rest, as in `וַיַּעֲבִירֵם` → *caused* ***them*** *to pass through*. Where none is, the pronoun answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside or beside its rendering; rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing the verb's own person and number, which is a subject, and never an object the Hebrew does not write, exactly as that rule leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added`. The verb's unit is discontinuous around such a pronoun under rule 25. **This applies only to a pronoun that truly supplies an object.** A reflexive pronoun the ASV uses to render the Hebrew verb's own voice or its elative sense is part of that verb's unit, because the source verb licenses it: `אִכַּף` → *bow myself* keeps *myself* with the Niphal verb and heads on *bow*, and `הִגְדִּיל עַל` → *magnified yourselves against* keeps *yourselves* with the Hiphil on the same ground. Position inside the English verb phrase is not what makes a word part of the verb's rendering — the complement, or the source verb's own voice or sense, must license it, and an unsupported object does not. **A supplied object noun is read on those same terms, and what decides it is whether the English noun writes the verb's own lexeme.** Where the ASV completes a Hebrew verb with an object noun the Hebrew does not write, run rule 31's subtraction on that noun. Where it does not carry the verb's lexeme, it answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering: `לֹא שָׁאָלוּ` → *asked* ***counsel*** *not* leaves *counsel* `added`, because `שָׁאַל` is the asking and *asked* has already written it, exactly as rule 17 leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added` and rule 20 a supplied lexical verb. Where it does carry the lexeme, the noun is part of that verb's one rendering, joins its unit, and the head goes by the same subtraction to whichever word carries the lexeme: `וַיַּעֲשׂוּ` → *did work* is one unit on the verb, headed on *did*, because `עָשָׂה` is the doing and the working alike and neither English word is a complement the other lacks. Read the source verb's lexeme rather than the English phrase's shape, since this rule's light-verb clause governs where the supplied noun is what carries that lexeme — `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel* heads on *counsel* — and this sentence governs where the verb's own English word has written it already. A supplied possessive standing on such a noun is disposed of by rule 18's closing sentence and is not made the verb's by the noun beside it. **But a preposition the ASV supplies to reach the verb's own object is part of that rendering.** Where the Hebrew writes a bare direct object — no object marker on it and no preposition of its own — and the English verb reaches that object through a preposition the ASV has written, the preposition belongs to the verb's unit and not to the object noun's: `חָמְסוּ תוֹרָתִי` → *have done violence* ***to*** *my law*, `תְּבַצְּעִי רֵעַיִךְ` → *hast greedily gained* ***of*** *thy neighbors*, `הֵקַלּוּ אָב וָאֵם` → *have set light* ***by*** *father and mother*, `אֲבַקֵּשׁ אִישׁ` → *sought* ***for*** *a man*, `טָחוּ תָּפֵל` → *have daubed ... with untempered mortar*. This is rule 16's reasoning where no marker stands to take the word: the same subtraction test finds that dropping it diminishes nothing but the object relation, and the object noun's own English is the noun. The unit is discontinuous under rule 25 where other material stands between the verb and the preposition, and the head is unaffected — it stays on the lexical verb, or on the complement where this rule's light-verb clause puts it. **And the object so reached may be a pronominal suffix on the verb rather than a noun.** Where a verbal object suffix stands with no preposition of its own and the English rendering reaches it through a supplied preposition — `יִבְּמָהּ` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *her*, `יַבְּמִי` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *me* — that preposition belongs to the verb's unit on exactly the terms just given, and the suffix keeps only the pronoun rule 18 writes for it. Do not read rule 18's *the English pronoun that realizes it* as reaching the preposition standing beside that pronoun: what that rule places is the pronoun, and a preposition the English verb's valency licenses is the verb's whether its object is a noun or a suffix. Rule 40 does not reach such a suffix either, since no preposition morpheme stands in the clause for the recasting to silence. Test by subtraction as before — drop the English preposition and ask whether anything but the object relation is diminished. Two limits. Where an object marker or a preposition of the object's own is present, that morpheme takes the word under rules 16 and 11, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And this does not touch rule 33: a function word supplied for an adverbial accusative is licensed by that noun's own case-function and stays with the noun, whereas a word supplied for a direct object is licensed by the English verb's valency, so read which the Hebrew noun is before placing it.
amendments.why: Rule 44's phrasal-particle sentence, read alone, folds any particle into the verb: it says such a pair is *one lexical verb plus its particle* and gives the subtraction only as a reason the head stays on the verb, never as a test of whether the particle belongs to the unit at all. ECC.3 met the case it had not considered. Seven particles in the chapter complete a lexeme the bare English verb does not write — *away*, *up*, *down*, *out*, *together*, and the *again* of שׁוּב → *turn ... again*, where *turn* alone is not returning — while the italicized *back* of ECC.3.22 יְבִיאֶנּוּ → *bring him back* adds a direction the Hebrew never wrote, since בּוֹא hiphil is the bringing and *bring* has already written it. The amendment adds no new doctrine: it applies the subtraction test rule 44 already runs on light-verb complements and on supplied object nouns to the particle as well, and routes the surplus to the same `added` under rule 30 that this rule already gives a supplied object and rule 17 a supplied lexical subject noun. It is worded to require that the bare English verb write the whole lexeme before a particle can be `added`, so the *put forth* and *take away* rulings are untouched; nothing in the corpus precedent shown contradicts it.

conventions: The `עֵת` refrain of ECC.3.1-8 divides three ways, and which one applies is read off the morphemes that are there. `עֵת` takes *a time* with the supplied indefinite article joining it under rule 15. A written `לְ` before the infinitive takes the *to* under rule 52. Where the construct governs a bare infinitive with no preposition — `עֵת סְפוֹד`, `עֵת רְקוֹד`, `עֵת כְּנוֹס` — the infinitive takes its own *to* under rule 52's closing sentence, which puts it on the same unit rule 19 would have. Where the rectum is a noun — `עֵת מִלְחָמָה` → *a time for war*, `עֵת שָׁלוֹם` → *a time for peace* — the recast relation *for* belongs to the rectum under rule 19. The construct `עֵת` takes only its own word in every one of the eight verses.

`אָמַרְתִּי אֲנִי` (ECC.3.17, ECC.3.18): the ASV writes one *I* where two morphemes could carry it, and the explicit pronoun `אֲנִי` takes it while the finite verb keeps only *said*. Both verses record the competing reading, which gives *I said* whole to the verb under rule 17 and marks the pronoun `unrepresented`.

Tripartite verbless clauses are settled by counting the ASV's predicative words against the morphemes standing in the clause. At ECC.3.13 one *is* is written and the predicate noun `מַתַּת` is free to take it, so rule 20's ruling applies and the resuming `הִיא` is its own `unrepresented` unit. At ECC.3.15 every predicate morpheme already holds English of its own — `הָיָה` → *hath been*, `כְּבָר` → *long ago* — so the further *is* of *That which is* falls to `הוּא`, the only morpheme left, exactly as the parallel second half of the verse puts its *is* on the written `לְ` under rule 49. Rule 20's tripartite sentence is not a direction to leave a resumptive pronoun unrendered wherever one stands; it governs the case where a predicate morpheme is available for the copula.

ECC.3.21 renders the attributive articles of `הָעֹלָה` and `הַיֹּרֶדֶת` by *whether*, the ASV recasting the attributive as an indirect question after *Who knoweth*. The article takes that word and heads on it under rule 41, since *whether* does the work rule 41 gives a relative; it is not `added` under rule 55 and the article is not left `unrepresented`. Rule 41's list of determiners was read as the words the ASV commonly writes rather than as a closed set, and the margin's *Or, that goeth* corroborates without deciding (rule 38).

Verb particles across the chapter are decided by one subtraction: *away* (3.5, 3.6), *up* (3.2, 3.3), *down* (3.3), *out* (3.11), *together* (3.5) and the *again* of `שׁוּב` → *turn ... again* (3.20) all join their verb's unit, because the bare English verb does not write the source lexeme without them; the italicized *back* of `יְבִיאֶנּוּ` → *bring him back* (3.22) is `added`, because `בּוֹא` hiphil is the bringing and *bring* has already written it. Rule 44 was amended on this chapter's evidence to carry that test.

Where an object marker or a preposition of the object's own is present, that morpheme takes the word under rules 16 and 11, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And this does not touch rule 33: a function word supplied for an adverbial accusative is licensed by that noun's own case-function and stays with the noun, whereas a word supplied for a direct object is licensed by the English verb's valency, so read which the Hebrew noun is before placing it.
amended.why: Rule 44's phrasal-particle sentence, read alone, folds any particle into the verb: it says such a pair is *one lexical verb plus its particle* and gives the subtraction only as a reason the head stays on the verb, never as a test of whether the particle belongs to the unit at all. ECC.3 met the case it had not considered. Seven particles in the chapter complete a lexeme the bare English verb does not write — *away*, *up*, *down*, *out*, *together*, and the *again* of שׁוּב → *turn ... again*, where *turn* alone is not returning — while the italicized *back* of ECC.3.22 יְבִיאֶנּוּ → *bring him back* adds a direction the Hebrew never wrote, since בּוֹא hiphil is the bringing and *bring* has already written it. The amendment adds no new doctrine: it applies the subtraction test rule 44 already runs on light-verb complements and on supplied object nouns to the particle as well, and routes the surplus to the same `added` under rule 30 that this rule already gives a supplied object and rule 17 a supplied lexical subject noun. It is worded to require that the bare English verb write the whole lexeme before a particle can be `added`, so the *put forth* and *take away* rulings are untouched; nothing in the corpus precedent shown contradicts it.

report: Checked all 36 candidate lemma groups plus a full read of the dump for `added` units, which the table is blind to. Every multi-treatment bucket is licensed by the English the ASV wrote rather than by a split analysis: הַ takes a written *the* and is unrepresented where none is written (rule 29); לְ before an infinitive takes a written *to*, a *that* where the clause is recast finitely (ECC.3.18), and nothing where the recasting writes no function word at all (ECC.3.14); וְ takes whichever connective the ASV wrote and is unrepresented at ECC.3.19 s006, where it wrote none (rule 14); כֹּל, טוֹב, אָדָם and בְּהֵמָה differ only in ASV rendering.

The עֵת refrain of ECC.3.1-8 divides three ways and all three are read off the Hebrew that is there: a written לְ takes the *to*; a bare infinitive construct after עֵת (עֵת סְפוֹד, עֵת רְקוֹד, עֵת כְּנוֹס) takes its own *to* under rule 52's closing sentence, which lands it on the same unit rule 19 would have; a nominal rectum takes the recast relation *for* under rule 19 (עֵת מִלְחָמָה → *a time for war*). The construct עֵת never holds the relational word in any of the eight verses. Recorded as a convention.

The one apparent outlier is the tripartite copula. ECC.3.13 marks the resuming הִיא `unrepresented` and sends the single *is* to the predicate noun under rule 20; ECC.3.15 gives *is* to הוּא. These are not two analyses of one construction. In 3.13 a predicate morpheme is free to take the one written copula, which is precisely the case rule 20 rules on; in 3.15 הָיָה already holds *hath been* and כְּבָר *long ago*, so the further *is* of *That which is* falls to the only morpheme left, exactly as the parallel second half puts its *is* on the written לְ under rule 49. Convention recorded rather than a patch.

Verb particles were checked as a group, since the table cannot see the `added` one. *away*, *up*, *down*, *out*, *together* and the *again* of שׁוּב → *turn ... again* all join their verbs' units; only the italicized *back* of ECC.3.22 יְבִיאֶנּוּ → *bring him back* is `added`. That is one subtraction test applied eight times, not two treatments — but rule 44's phrasal-particle sentence, read alone, would have folded *back* in too, so rule 44 is amended to carry the test it already applies to supplied object nouns.

BSB disagreements: no genuine error. The Td x 21 and R x 5 blocks are the documented convention difference (BSB attaches the article and the preposition to the host word). ECC.3.13 הִיא is directly ruled by rule 20's tripartite sentence. ECC.3.17 אֶת is rule 16's ordinary unrepresented marker. ECC.3.18 הֶם is the reflexive dative rule 40 names, with the ASV's two pronouns going to the two independent pronouns הֶם and הֵמָּה. ECC.3.19 וּ has no connective written for it. ECC.3.21 בְּנֵי is genuinely dropped, the ASV compressing *the sons of men* to *man*, and the margin's literal gloss corroborates without deciding (rules 22 and 38).

The closest thing to a real error is ECC.3.11 בְּלִי, which BSB represents. The clause writes four subordinating or negative morphemes (מִן, בְּלִי, אֲשֶׁר, לֹא) against two English words, *so that* and *cannot*. The chapter gives *so that* to the privative מִן (rule 48) and *cannot* to לֹא, which the corpus aligns to *cannot* headed on it in fourteen units (rule 35), leaving בְּלִי and אֲשֶׁר as the unrendered occurrences of a doubled negation and a doubled complementizer. Rule 48's negative-substantive sentence would instead put the negation on בְּלִי, but that sentence governs a clause with no other negative morpheme in it. The verse note names the competing reading; left as accepted.

ECC.3.21 renders two attributive articles by *whether*, which is not one of the words rule 41 enumerates. The article was given the word rather than left unrepresented with *whether* `added` under rule 55, because *whether* does the subordinating work rule 41 gives a relative. That is one verse and two tokens with no corpus support shown, so it is recorded as a convention and not promoted; a later chapter meeting the same construction can decide whether rule 41's list is closed.
